newsitem.title: USA: Sales of previously owned homes fell in March.
newsitem.headline: Sales of previously owned homes fell in March.

text.p: Sales of existing homes fell in March from a near-record pace the month before, an industry group said Friday, hurt by higher interest rates and bad weather.
The National Association of Realtors said sales of existing homes fell 2.8 percent in March to a seasonably adjusted annual rate of 4.11 million units from a revised 4.23 million in February.

In February, the pace of sales jumped to its second highest level on record. The group attributed the drop in March sales to bad weather in some parts of the country and to an increase in interest rates.

"The activity we are seeing now is beginning to reflect the impact of bad weather, including massive flooding in the Midwest and West, which has diverted attention from home ownership to survival," association President Russell Booth said.
Booth said the March slowdown indicates the housing market is "leveling out to a more normal pattern of activity."
"It seems as if housing still has a good deal of momentum," said Ken Mayland, chief economist at KeyCorp in Cleveland. "We've gone from a very strong level of activity to a strong level of activity."

But Mayland voiced concern about how much of an impact a weakening stock market could have on home sales. He noted that the housing market's ongoing strength in recent months was due in part to the wealth created by rising stock prices.
"If the stock market falters more this year ... that would indicate a bigger risk for the whole housing (sector)," he said.

The realtors' report showed the median price for an existing home -- half sold above that and half below -- rose to $120,000 in March from $117,500 in February. The median stood at $115,700 a year ago.
Rates for a 30-year mortgage loan averaged 7.90 percent in March, up from 7.65 percent in February and 7.62 percent in March 1996.
The group said it does not anticipate any major swings in interest rates for the remainder of the year.
There were 2.35 million existing homes available at the end of March, representing a 6.9-month supply at the current pace of sales.

One economist expressed concern about the rising number of homes available for sale, noting the impact the inventory levels could have on the broader housing sector if sales continue to slow in the months ahead.

"If it continues to build at the (current) rate, all of that inventory on the market will start to spill over to new home sales and affect housing values," said Paul Taylor, senior economist at America's Community Bankers, a Washington-based trade association.
"We're concerned about it because everybody expects this market to slow down this year," Taylor added.

During March, sales for existing homes rose 1.6 percent in the Northeast to 640,000 a year, while in the South, the nation's biggest regional housing market, they were unchanged at a rate of 1.53 million.
In the Midwest, March sales dropped 8.3 percent to a rate of 1. million units and in the West they fell 5.1 percent to 930,000 units.
